lesson.title: Fear of the Foreign: Nativism in a Changing America
lesson.summary: In the years after World War I, many native-born white Protestant Americans grew fearful that immigration and radical politics were eroding the country they knew, fueling a powerful wave of nativism.
lesson.body:
Nativism is the belief that native-born people and their customs deserve favored treatment over immigrants, and it surged in the United States in the years following World War I. The country had just lived through the New Immigration Wave, a decades-long surge of newcomers, many of them Italians, Jews from Russia and Poland, Greeks, and other southern and eastern Europeans, who differed in religion, language, and custom from the earlier immigrants from Britain, Germany, and Scandinavia. To many older-stock Americans, these newer arrivals seemed harder to absorb into American life, and that unease hardened into organized hostility.

That hostility fed directly on the fears of the first Red Scare. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 brought a communist government to power, and after a wave of anarchist bombings struck the United States in 1919, including an explosion at the Washington home of Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, many Americans came to associate immigrants, particularly those from eastern and southern Europe, with political radicalism. Palmer responded with a series of raids in late 1919 and early 1920 that rounded up thousands of suspected radicals, many of them immigrants, for deportation. In the public imagination, being foreign and being dangerous became closely linked.

Pseudo-scientific ideas lent this prejudice a veneer of respectability. The eugenics movement, popular among some scientists and policymakers of the era, ranked ethnic groups by supposed biological fitness and warned that unrestricted immigration would weaken the American population. The case of Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, two Italian immigrant anarchists arrested in 1920 and convicted in 1921 of a Massachusetts robbery and murder on evidence that many contemporaries and later historians found troubling, became a lightning rod. To their supporters, the two men were victims of anti-immigrant and anti-radical prejudice; to their opponents, they were dangerous foreign agitators who deserved punishment. Their execution in 1927 remains debated by historians to this day.

By the early 1920s, nativist organizations, labor unions worried about wage competition, and sympathetic members of Congress had built enough pressure to break with the nation's long tradition of largely open immigration. That pressure would soon produce the first hard numerical limits on who could enter the United States, a shift explored in the next chapter on the Emergency Quota Act.
